Why Your Drywall Cracks Keep Coming Back

If you have filled the same crack three times, the problem is not the filler. It is that filling was never the repair.

March 4, 2026 · 6 min read

Recurring cracks are the single most common drywall complaint in this valley, and there are only really three explanations. Working out which one you have determines whether the fix is an afternoon or a much bigger conversation.

Cause 1: it was never repaired, only filled

This is most of them. Someone pushed spackle into the crack, sanded it, painted it, and it looked perfect for six months. But a crack in drywall is almost always a seam — the joint where two sheets meet, covered by paper or mesh tape. When that tape fails, filler on top of it is cosmetic. It bridges nothing.

The real repair means cutting the failed tape out, re-taping the joint, and floating the compound wide — eight to twelve inches either side, feathered to nothing — so no single line carries the stress. Then texture, then prime. That crack does not come back.

Cause 2: normal seasonal movement

Contra Costa sits on expansive clay soil. It swells through the wet winter and shrinks through the dry summer, and houses move with it — a few millimetres, invisibly, every year. Add wood framing that expands and contracts with humidity and you get hairline cracks that open in August and close in February.

This is especially pronounced on hillside lots in Lafayette, Orinda and Moraga. A properly taped and widely floated repair with mesh reinforcement handles this well — the movement gets distributed across a wide float instead of concentrating on one line.

Cause 3: the crack is a symptom

Some cracks are your house reporting a structural problem. The warning signs are worth knowing:

  • Cracks wider than about a quarter inch
  • Diagonal cracks running from door or window corners that keep widening year over year
  • Doors and windows that have started sticking in the same part of the house
  • Cracks accompanied by sloping or bouncing floors
  • Horizontal cracking on a garage or basement wall

Any of those and the drywall is not the problem. Patch it and it will reopen, because the cause is under the house rather than in the wall. That is a structural engineer or foundation contractor conversation, and a drywall contractor who tells you otherwise is selling you a repair that is guaranteed to fail.

The specific case of the wall-to-ceiling joint

A crack running along the line where the wall meets the ceiling, usually on an upper floor, is extremely common in Walnut Creek and Concord homes from the 1950s to 70s. It is often truss uplift — roof trusses flexing seasonally and pulling the ceiling up away from the wall.

Re-taping it rigidly will just crack again next year. The better answers are a flexible detail at the joint, or crown molding fastened only to the wall so the ceiling can move behind it. It is one of the few cases where trim genuinely beats mud.

What a lasting repair looks like

  1. Cut the failed tape and loose material out — do not fill over it
  2. Re-tape the joint, mesh where movement is expected
  3. Float three coats, each wider than the last, feathered to nothing
  4. Sand, match the existing texture
  5. Prime before paint so the sheen matches

If your crack has come back more than once, send us a photo. Half the time we can tell you from the picture whether you have a taping problem or a foundation one.
